markscheme_points.text: hadron: neutron/proton and lepton: electron/(electron) neutrino

hints: Hint 1: Think about the two families - one family is made of quarks and feels the strong force inside the nucleus, the other family is fundamental and includes the particle orbiting the atom.
parts.proper_answer: a hadron: proton (or neutron); a lepton: electron (or electron neutrino).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sort Particles Into Two Families**
Think of all particles as belonging to two big groups. Hadrons are not fundamental - they are made of quarks and they feel the strong nuclear force. Leptons are fundamental - they are not made of quarks and they do not feel the strong force.

Step 2: **Pick Familiar Examples**
The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, both made of quarks, so both are hadrons. Around the nucleus are electrons, which are fundamental and not made of quarks, so electrons are leptons. The neutrino is another lepton.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: Describe, in terms of the simple quark model,

markscheme_points.text: proton: up up down or uud

hints: Hint 1: Remember a proton is a baryon, so it contains three quarks using only up and down flavours, and the total charge must add to $+1e$ where up is $+2/3e$ and down is $-1/3e$.
parts.proper_answer: proton is $uud$ (two up quarks and one down quark).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use The Simple Quark Model**
In this model, protons and neutrons are baryons, meaning they are each made of three quarks. At AS level you only need up ($u$) quarks with charge $+2/3e$ and down ($d$) quarks with charge $-1/3e$.

Step 2: **Build Charge +1**
A proton has charge $+1e$. The only combination that works is: $$ (+2/3e) + (+2/3e) + (-1/3e) = +1e $$ That is two up quarks and one down quark, written as $uud$.

walkthrough:
Step 1: **Keep The Baryon Rule**
A neutron is also a baryon made of three quarks, again only up and down flavours in this simple model.

Step 2: **Build Charge Zero**
A neutron has zero charge. The only combination that works is: $$ (+2/3e) + (-1/3e) + (-1/3e) = 0 $$ That is one up quark and two down quarks, written as $udd$.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem: Beta particles may be emitted during the decay of an unstable nucleus of an atom. The emission of a beta particle is due to the decay of a neutron.
parts.text: Complete the following word equation for the particles produced in this reaction.
hints: Hint 1: Start from a neutral neutron decaying to a positively charged proton plus a negatively charged beta particle (electron) - think what third invisible particle is needed to conserve energy and lepton number.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall Beta-Minus Decay**
A beta particle is a fast-moving electron emitted from the nucleus. It does not come from the shells - it is created when a neutron changes into a proton inside the nucleus.

Step 2: **Complete The Equation**
Charge must balance: $0 \rightarrow +1 -1$, so proton + electron already balances charge. To conserve energy, momentum and lepton number, a third particle is also emitted: $$ \text{neutron} \rightarrow \text{proton} + \text{electron} + \text{electron antineutrino} $$

key_concepts: beta-minus decay of neutron
conservation of charge and lepton number, antineutrino

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: State the change in quark composition of the particles during this reaction.

markscheme_points.text: up down down (quarks) change to up up down (quarks) or down (quark) changes to up (quark)

hints: Hint 1: Compare your quark combinations for neutron and proton from part (b) - focus on which single quark flavour must flip for the baryon to change from neutral to charge $+1$.
parts.proper_answer: $udd$ changes to $uud$ (a down quark changes to an up quark).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Nucleon Change To Quark Change**
From (b), neutron is $udd$ and proton is $uud$. The decay neutron to proton must therefore involve a change inside the quark structure.

Step 2: **Identify The Flavour Change**
Comparing $udd \rightarrow uud$, one $d$ quark has become a $u$ quark: $$ d \rightarrow u $$ This flavour change is a weak interaction effect, with the charge increase of $+1e$ carried away by the emitted electron.
